source.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

candidates.name: reinforcement learning
candidates.summary: A learning paradigm in which an agent takes actions and optimizes its behavior to maximize cumulative reward received from an environment. Feedback is a scalar signal rather than labeled target outputs.
candidates.evidence: the reasoning abilities of LLMs can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning (RL)

candidates.name: Group Relative Policy Optimization
candidates.summary: A policy-gradient algorithm that samples a group of outputs per prompt and computes each output's advantage by normalizing its reward against the group's mean and standard deviation. It removes the need for a learned value model and uses PPO-style clipping and a KL penalty.
candidates.evidence: GRPO samples a group of outputs {o1, o2, · · · , oG} from the old policy

candidates.name: Proximal Policy Optimization
candidates.summary: A policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that limits each update by clipping the ratio between new and old policy probabilities. It typically uses a learned value model and generalized advantage estimation.
candidates.evidence: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), which is widely used in the RL stage of LLMs

candidates.name: advantage estimation
candidates.summary: The advantage measures how much better an action or output is than a baseline expectation, reducing variance in policy-gradient updates. It can be computed with a learned value function (as in GAE) or from group-normalized rewards.
candidates.evidence: the advantage is typically computed by applying the Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)

candidates.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
candidates.summary: A measure of how one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution. In RL fine-tuning it is used as a penalty to keep the trained policy close to a reference policy.
candidates.evidence: an unbiased estimator of the KL divergence (Schulman, 2020) is directly added in the loss

candidates.name: rule-based reward
candidates.summary: A reward computed by deterministic checks such as answer matching, compiler tests or format checks, rather than by a learned model. It gives objective feedback on tasks with verifiable outcomes.
candidates.evidence: we employ rule-based rewards to deliver precise feedback for data in mathematical, coding, and logical reasoning domains

candidates.name: reward hacking
candidates.summary: When a policy exploits flaws or biases in a reward function to obtain high reward without achieving the intended goal. It is more likely with learned reward models as optimization proceeds.
candidates.evidence: neural reward models are susceptible to reward hacking during large-scale reinforcement learning

candidates.name: chain-of-thought reasoning
candidates.summary: Having a language model produce intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer, which improves performance on complex tasks. It can be elicited by few-shot examples or prompts like 'think step by step'.
candidates.evidence: chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting

candidates.name: supervised fine-tuning
candidates.summary: Further training a pretrained model on curated input-output pairs with a supervised (cross-entropy) objective so it imitates the desired outputs.
candidates.evidence: we bypass the conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase before RL training

candidates.name: knowledge distillation
candidates.summary: Training a smaller student model to reproduce the behavior of a larger teacher, here by fine-tuning on outputs generated by the teacher.
candidates.evidence: we adopt a model distillation approach, a well-established technique for efficient knowledge transfer

candidates.name: rejection sampling
candidates.summary: Generating many candidate outputs and keeping only those that pass a filter, such as correctness or readability checks, to build a training set.
candidates.evidence: performing rejection sampling from the checkpoint of the first-stage RL training

candidates.name: test-time compute scaling
candidates.summary: Improving model performance by spending more computation at inference, for example by generating longer reasoning or sampling multiple answers.
candidates.evidence: Scaling Inference-time Compute

candidates.name: self-consistency decoding
candidates.summary: Sampling several reasoning paths for a question and choosing the most frequent final answer to improve accuracy.
candidates.evidence: by leveraging the self-consistency decoding (Wang et al., 2023c)

candidates.name: pass@k evaluation
candidates.summary: A metric that samples k responses per problem and measures correctness; pass@1 averages the correctness of individual samples, while pass@k counts a problem solved if any of k samples is correct.
candidates.evidence: pass@1 = 1/k Σ p_i, where p_i denotes the correctness of the i-th response

candidates.name: process reward model
candidates.summary: A learned reward model that scores intermediate reasoning steps rather than only the final outcome.
candidates.evidence: Process Reward Model (PRM) PRM is a reasonable method to guide the model toward better approaches

candidates.name: Monte Carlo tree search
candidates.summary: A search algorithm that explores a decision tree by sampling simulated rollouts and using their results to guide further expansion, often with a value model.
candidates.evidence: we explored using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to enhance test-time compute scalability

candidates.name: mixture-of-experts
candidates.summary: A neural architecture where a router activates only a subset of expert sub-networks per token, so total parameters greatly exceed those used per token.
candidates.evidence: Built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, DeepSeek V3 has 671 billion total parameters, with 37 billion activated per token

candidates.name: LLM-as-a-judge
candidates.summary: Using a language model to evaluate or grade other model outputs, for example scoring correctness or comparing two responses.
candidates.evidence: employing LLM as judges

candidates.name: preference reward model
candidates.summary: A model trained on pairs of responses ranked by preference to output a scalar score approximating human preference, used as an RL reward.
candidates.evidence: we first generate preference pairs by prompting DeepSeek-V3 using the arena-hard prompt format

candidates.name: reinforcement learning from human feedback
candidates.summary: Aligning a language model by training a reward model on human preference data and optimizing the model against it with RL.
candidates.evidence: A prominent instantiation of this approach is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

candidates.name: benchmark data contamination
candidates.summary: Overlap between training data and evaluation data that inflates benchmark scores. It is mitigated by filtering, for example removing texts with n-gram matches to test questions.
candidates.evidence: we implemented comprehensive decontamination procedures for both pre-training and post-training data

candidates.name: emergent reasoning behavior
candidates.summary: Capabilities such as reflection, verification and exploring alternatives that appear during training without being explicitly taught, often alongside longer outputs.
candidates.evidence: DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits an “aha moment” (Table 2)

candidates.name: language consistency reward
candidates.summary: A reward term giving the fraction of words in a reasoning chain that are in the target language, used to discourage mixing languages.
candidates.evidence: calculated as the proportion of target language words in the CoT

candidates.name: jailbreak attack
candidates.summary: A prompting technique that tries to circumvent a model's safety alignment to elicit harmful output.
candidates.evidence: Robustness against Jailbreaking
